Fox News Digital's Charles Creitz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump trade chief reveals what preceded Canada walking away from 'best deal in the world'
articles.summary: Jamieson Greer says Canada walked away from a handshake deal with President Trump on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, then demanded even more.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's top trade advisor, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, said Canada walked away from the "best deal in the world" after the nation declined to finalize a trade agreement with the U.S. nearly two weeks ago. Greer joined "Special Report" on Thursday to detail the negotiations that preceded the contentious trade fight between the U.S. and its northern neighbor. "We offered them the best deal. They looked at it square in the face and turned around," he said on "Special Report." Greer’s comments come amid a fierce trade war between the U.S. and Canada that Trump further escalated by signing an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America." TRUMP'S CANADA TARIFF FIGHT REACHES CRITICAL POINT AS HOUSE GOP SUMMONS TRADE CHIEF The trade chief said that although Trump’s trade program already gives Canada "the best deal," U.S. officials were willing to negotiate after Canadian authorities approached the administration seeking a revised agreement. "I told them what we could deliver. I said, ‘We could try to give you the best deal in the world on steel, aluminum, autos and help you out on lumber,’" Greer told Fox News. "These are things very sensitive for the Canadians, and we managed to move the levers of our government to give them that deal." FEARS OF A CANADIAN TRADE WAR ARE OVERBLOWN. SO FAR, IT’S MORE OF A SKIRMISH After Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney reached the handshake agreement, Canadian officials returned to Ottawa. Greer said he remains unsure what transpired there that ultimately prompted Canada to renege on the deal and seek additional concessions. "When they came back, they wanted more, they wanted more tariff relief. It wasn't good enough to have the best deal in the world," he told Fox News chief political anchor Bret Baier. "They wanted it to be even better… These are things we couldn't accommodate." DAVID MARCUS: CANADA SEES TRUMP TRADE WAR AS ‘LIFE AND DEATH’ WHILE AMERICANS BARELY NOTICE Canada suspended trade talks on Aug. 21. U.S. trade officials blamed the breakdown on what they described as "new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada" that "upended the careful balance" of the negotiations. "We were ready to do it. We gave them the best deal in the world. Did it give them everything? No. Did we have everything we wanted? No. That's how a deal works," Greer said. ‘CAPTAIN CANADA’ FIREBRAND UNLOADS ON TRUMP WITH PROFANE ONE-LINER AS TRADE WAR ESCALATES The trade chief said Canadian leaders appeared on television after the agreement fell apart and claimed the country had "been attacked." Greer pushed back on that characterization, arguing that the "vast majority" of Canadian goods enter the U.S. duty-free and noting that Canada, along with China, are the only countries to have retaliated against U.S. trade measures. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Since even before the second Trump term, they've limited our ability to sell dairy into Canada, and they're importing things from China," he said. "They're turning them into other goods and trying to get them duty-free across our border." Greer, who believes the Canadians were negotiating in good faith, said he has received some outreach from Canada but no formal negotiations since Aug. 21. As for what comes next, Greer said the trade deal’s future now lies "in Canada’s corner."

articles.title: Ted Cruz names ‘most powerful Democrat’ as he warns socialist rise has paralyzed bipartisanship
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz claims Chuck Schumer is "truly terrified" of the extreme left, warning that progressive momentum is paralyzing bipartisan work.
articles.body: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, believes that fear of a rising wave of progressives is paralyzing possible bipartisan work on permitting reform that would otherwise create fertile ground for collaboration. "That dynamic is dangerous right now because they are terrified of the extreme left. Finding a middle ground on ideological issues right now is … the prospects for success, particularly between now and election day, are not high," Cruz said at an energy summit hosted by Club for Growth and Arnold Ventures on Thursday. "Schumer is truly terrified right now," he added, referring to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Cruz’s political assessment underscores what progressive momentum in the 2026 midterms means for more establishment figures in the Democratic Party — and especially the ones already in Congress — and the policy areas that legislators may still want to address before the November midterm elections. CRUZ SAYS MAMDANI, AOC, PLATNER SHOW DEMOCRATS' LEFTWARD SHIFT: 'THAT'S WHERE THE ENERGY IS' "They’re in the middle of a revolution," Cruz said. "Their problem is that they’re very driven by their interest groups. They’re captured by their activists." His remarks came as he delivered an address at an energy affordability summit hosted by the Club for Growth, a free-market group that advocates for limited government. In particular, the event centered on permitting reform, an area where Democrats and Republicans have found some overlap. Although differences remain about just how far to scale back regulations or how far to push legislative changes, lawmakers at the event stressed that bipartisan work on cutting back red tape could meaningfully expand American access to energy projects domestically. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, noted how regulatory bodies had prevented the expansion of nuclear energy — a source of power that is uniting Republicans and Democrats as a new frontier in a space apart from fossil fuels. "We have built three new nuclear reactors in like the last 40 years. It went quickly from: we didn’t even know about the technology, to 20% of U.S. electric generation from nuclear reactors," Wright said. 100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY "We created the Nuclear Regulatory Commission… in the name of safety, no malintent. But since that creation, we’ve built almost no reactors in the United States since. If it’s so uncertain and so long to permit something, it’s just not worth investing in. That’s awful! Nuclear is just an awesome energy technology." Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio., stressed that many of the discussions around reform have come down to a matter of practical details. "There's a lot of conversations going on not about who's going to fight with whom or who is going to take credit for it, but rather what is the mechanics of getting it done," Moreno said at the Club for Growth event. "When it comes to permitting reform, if we can actually pull this off, Scott, what does it mean? It means lower energy prices for all Americans, us taking better care of our environment, being good stewards for the next generation. Those are worthy goals that should unite all of us, and I'm hopeful that we can get that done," Moreno said, speaking to conservative political commentator Scott Jennings, a moderator at the event. Despite a sense of optimism among several speakers — and even from Cruz himself — Cruz warned listeners that progressives already have a very real presence inside the Capitol that casts a shadow on permitting reform and other areas. "It is not the case that every Senate Democrat is a Marxist or Islamist. What is the case is that every Senate Democrat is terrified of the Marxists and Islamists. Because that’s where the energy is in their party, that’s where the power is, that’s where the money is; it's where the young people are. I think Mamdani is the single most powerful Democrat in the country," Cruz said, referring to the socialist mayor of New York City. Since Mamdani, a self-proclaimed socialist, came to power earlier this year, a series of progressive candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have won key primary races and even toppled veteran incumbents. A few notable races include New York's socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier and her victory over incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., the veteran chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. Along those lines, Melat Kiros, another socialist in Colorado, unseated 30-year incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Colo. SCHUMER DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER DSA BELONGS IN DEMOCRATIC PARTY With pressures like that, Cruz argued that it’s difficult to find legislators who are willing to separate themselves from progressives. He believes there isn’t leadership to push back against that progressive momentum. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Look, Schumer is known for a lot of things but acts of principle and courage are not among them," Cruz said.

articles.title: Denmark says it hopes to start deporting migrants to non-EU 'return hubs' as early as next year
articles.summary: Denmark said it hoped to begin sending rejected asylum seekers to non-European Union “return hubs” as early as 2027, ahead of a Friday meeting of five countr...
articles.body:
Denmark said it hoped to begin sending rejected asylum seekers to non-European Union "return hubs" as early as 2027, ahead of a Friday meeting of five countries leading European efforts to establish such centers outside the continent.

In June, European lawmakers voted to allow member states to set up migrant detention centers outside the EU, known as "return hubs." Any EU nation can now negotiate on its own or in small coalitions to deport migrants not to their home countries but to facilities yet to be built in third countries, outside the 27-nation bloc.

"We cannot accept that people without a legal stay continue to reside in our respective countries," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said on Friday as he welcomed ministers from Germany, Austria, The Netherlands and Greece to Copenhagen to discuss progress on establishing the deportation centers outside Europe.

"And at the same time we would like to work together with third countries to be able to give irregular migrants a second chance in a partner country," Rasmussen said.

The five countries have been negotiating with governments mainly in Africa to host sites to hold rejected asylum seekers, pioneering the initiative for the whole of the EU.

In an interview with Danish broadcaster DR published on Friday, Denmark's Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov said he hoped that the non-EU return hubs would already be in place in 2027. Bødskov said talks with non-EU countries had reached a crucial phase.

"Today we take the next step, here today with my European colleagues, to realize return hubs as soon as possible in the upcoming years," Bart van den Brink, Austria's asylum and migration minister, said in Copenhagen.

In early August, a spokesperson for the Rwandan government told local media that "it was natural" for her government to negotiate with European countries and others to potentially host asylum seekers who are not allowed to live elsewhere.

Migrant rights group have criticized European efforts to set up deportation centers abroad where it may be difficult to monitor and enforce human rights compliance.

In an emailed statement, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, said "vague assurances of compliance with human rights law are not enough."

"States need to commit to the guardrails necessary to prevent setting up human rights black holes," he said.

Brussels-based rights group PICUM condemned the meeting in Copenhagen.

"EU leaders may call these centers an "innovative solution," but outsourcing migration control is an old tactic to simply move people out of sight and evade human rights obligations," the group's director Michele LeVoy said.

AP journalist Philipp Jenne in Vienna and Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed to this report.

articles.title: Rubber meets the road in mail-in ballot fight
articles.summary: In today’s issue: Time is quickly running short on the Trump administration’s ability to implement President Trump’s push to restrict mail-in ballots as his executive order remains mired in a court battle. The midterm voting period officially kicks off today as election officials in North Carolina can start sending out mail-in ballots to voters who request them, under state law. The state elections…
articles.body:
Time is quickly running short on the Trump administration’s ability to implement President Trump ’s push to restrict mail-in ballots as his executive order remains mired in a court battle.

The midterm voting period officially kicks off today as election officials in North Carolina can start sending out mail-in ballots to voters who request them, under state law.

The state elections board has a special meeting planned for 9 a.m. to discuss possible new guidance on mail-in voting but so far hasn’t released the potential rules changes that it’s considering.

That caused frustration from North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein (D), who called on the board to “get it together.”

“No one should have to ask these questions less than 48 hours before absentee ballots are mailed out,” he said in a post on the social platform X .

Still, state elections board spokesperson Jason Tyson told Carolina Public Press on Thursday that they have “no current plans” to use the portal that the Postal Service has set up for carrying out the order.

The administration is currently appealing a federal judge’s ruling blocking it from moving forward with voting restrictions at least for one more week. The Department of Justice asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to lift the block.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani , who issued the two-week pause, separately held a hearing Thursday to determine whether to block the plan indefinitely. She hasn’t issued a ruling yet.

At issue is whether the U.S. Postal Service can carry out a rule from Trump’s order directing that mail-in ballots only be sent to people on a list of eligible voters provided by states to the federal government. Under Trump’s order, the Postal Service would not deliver mail-in ballots to those not on the list or ballots that don’t meet certain design requirements, including unique barcodes for tracking.

But while the legal battle has bounced from court to court, the window has been closing on the time needed to implement the order even if the courts were to uphold it.

Today marks 60 days before Election Day — the same number of days in advance that states would have to have submitted their voter lists by under Trump’s executive order.

While North Carolina is the only state that could send ballots as soon as today — another 18 states start sending ballots around 45 days before an election — this 60-day timeline affects even the states that don’t plan to send out their mail-in ballots for another month.

That would likely require the Postal Service to adjust its policy if the order were to be upheld, and even then, the time to carry all this out would be extremely limited.

Courts also tend to be hesitant about making major changes to election administration too close to Election Day unless an urgent situation warrants it.

The Postal Service also appears to be dealing with other logistical difficulties toward implementing the order beyond the court battles. A whistleblower report released earlier this week cast doubt about the functionality of the portal that was created to help carry out the order.

The whistleblower alleged the system has many flaws because of its “rushed” development, which included the elimination of a standard testing period.

▪ Bloomberg : Why Trump’s war on mail-in voting risks backfiring.

▪ CNN : Election officials say they can’t comply with Trump’s mail-in ballot rules.

The Missouri Supreme Court has blocked a GOP-passed congressional map from going into effect in November, ruling unanimously that a referendum intended to overrule the map could go on the ballot in November. The decision effectively saves Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) district and makes him a favorite to win reelection.

Trump announced Adam Telle , the current assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, will serve as acting Army secretary in the aftermath of Dan Driscoll’s resignation from the post. Telle is assuming the role “effective immediately.”

Fox News announced it has parted ways with longtime host Maria Bartiromo , giving few details about what led to her departure in a short statement. The network thanked Bartiromo for her past 12 and a half years working at Fox and wished her “all the best on her next chapter.” She had been one of Trump’s strongest defenders at Fox.

EARLY RELEASE : House Republican leadership announced Thursday it would cancel the final two weeks of its September session, ending the legislative calendar early before the midterms.

Lawmakers are heading out of town ahead of the Labor Day weekend and won’t return until the next Monday, Sept. 14 — the same day that the Senate will return from its monthlong recess. The House will be in session through that week, but now members will return home for the last two weeks of the month.

Members of both parties are eager to focus on campaigning ahead of the midterms as they battle for control of both chambers of Congress.

The House was able to pass the short-term funding measure to keep the government open past the midterms through Dec. 11, which Trump signed into law Wednesday, but it wasn’t expected to advance much other significant business with time winding down and a razor-thin majority.

The House Republican whip’s office said members could still be called back to Washington during those two weeks with 48 hours’ notice if the Senate approves what would be a party-line budget reconciliation package, which would provide additional funding for the Iran war, among other initiatives. The Hill’s Mike Lillis reports that House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries ’s (D-N.Y.) tone dramatically changed Thursday after he met with Democratic Reps. Jeffries and his deputies had initially suggested the move warranted a “significant response,” while some Democrats wanted the two of them to lose their committee posts. But the leader said he and the two members came away from their meeting agreeing to communicate “in a consistent way where we can arrive at shared priorities.”

He said rank-and-file Democrats will continue to discuss possible changes to internal caucus rules in response to the defections, but he suggested Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez will not be punished.

Multiple outlets reported Christian Castro has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators about shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg during the enforcement surge in January.

Castro was previously arrested in Texas after he was charged in Minnesota with second-degree assault with a deadly weapon and falsely reporting a crime. But he was released from jail last week as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) said he wasn’t obligated to extradite Castro to Minnesota authorities while the Texas secretary of state’s office reviews the case.

Sosa-Celis had initially been accused of beating an officer with a broom handle and snow shovel, but the charges were dropped after video evidence showed the officers might have lied about the encounter, The Associated Press reported.

The federal indictment against Castro hadn’t been unsealed as of late Thursday.

Steinem was remembered as a trailblazer who was critical to the women’s rights movement.

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton , the first woman to serve as a major party presidential nominee, phoned in to “CBS Mornings,” calling Steinem the “architect” of women’s equality.

“Oh, Gayle, I’m heartsick, as I think everyone who not only knew her but followed her, was inspired and challenged by her,” Clinton said.

The former first lady credited Steinem with creating opportunities for women over the course of decades, including for Sally Ride to become the first American woman to go into space and for Title IX to be passed.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), the first female House Speaker, said Steinem “changed what was possible for women in America.”

“As we honor her extraordinary life, we must teach the next generation about the barriers she broke and to remain relentless in our pursuit of equality—just as Gloria would want us to be,” she said in a post on X .

Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex , remembered working with Steinem to encourage more young voters to become politically active and getting to know her on a personal level.

Former President Obama , who awarded Steinem the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013, said she helped awaken the world to the problems of domestic violence, lack of affordable childcare and unfair hiring practices.

A wide range of celebrities, including Oprah Winfrey and Billie Jean King , also praised the activist and icon.

The ban applies for 2-year-olds in pre-school through the last year of middle school in eighth grade. A “small” number of high school classrooms, up to five per school, will have access to AI pilot programs under the “direct supervision” of a teacher, Mamdani’s office said.

Public high school students will also take two AI critical thinking classes during the 2026-2027 academic year. The use of AI chatbots will be prohibited across all grades.

Mamdani said children need teachers and “human connection” to learn and grow in classrooms.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI in early education is not only inevitable, but that it is necessary. We do not see it that way,” he said at a press conference.

Mamdani’s action is one of the latest instances of officials taking action to limit the impacts of the development of artificial intelligence and technology on youth. Many states have passed restrictions on the use of cellphones during the school day.

He’s not alone in taking action on AI, as officials in Los Angeles also announced that they would significantly restrict the use of AI at all grade levels.

Harriet Tubman was set to appear on the front of the $20 bill in place of Andrew Jackson, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced in July after a series of delays that the department had scrapped plans to do so .

First lady Martha Washington is the only woman so far to have appeared as the primary portrait on U.S. paper currency, appearing on a $1 silver certificate from the late 19th century to mid-20th century.

articles.title: Never mind vaccines — America can’t even track dangerous diseases
articles.summary: A country that needed 2,900 cases and two deaths to register a disease it eliminated a generation ago is not prepared.
articles.body:
Pennsylvania recorded its first measles deaths in 35 years this week, and the national count of cases has passed 2,900 — more than in any year since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000 .

The argument that followed was about vaccines, and they do matter, but that is yesterday’s fight. The failure that should keep Congress up at night is quieter: the U.S. still cannot see, in one place and in near real-time, what is happening biologically inside its own borders.

I built disease detection systems for the Defense Threat Reduction Agency , ran hospital epidemiology at Michigan State University, and worked on national security problems at Sandia National Laboratories. The hardest problem was never the sequencing or the software. It was that no two data sources described the same disease the same way.

Each state keeps its own list of reportable conditions and its own case definitions. Each laboratory and hospital keeps its own data format. Before a single alert can fire, someone must build a translation layer that aligns those schemas and vocabularies into one picture. In the Army, we called that a common operating picture. American public health does not have one, and no one oversees building it.

This is not an attack on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — in fact, the agency says so itself. It “ does not have direct authority to require data reporting, ” according to its website, and receives data from 50 states and more than 3,000 local jurisdictions, each with its own data-sharing agreement.

Case notification to the national system is voluntary , and national counts are provisional and revised weekly . Jurisdictions still send case reports in several technical standards; the CDC is still working toward a single one . The picture is scattered across the the Food and Drug Administration and the Departments of Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, Agriculture and Defense, as well as the states. No one is assigned to assemble it.

We know what works, because we have watched it work. When Medicare made weekly reporting of respiratory illness and bed capacity a condition of participation in November 2024 , the requirement reached essentially every hospital in the country.

When bird flu spread through dairy herds in 2024, voluntary testing enrolled 75 of the nation’s roughly 36,000 dairy farms , while influenza virus turned up in 36 percent of retail milk samples , including in five states with no reported outbreak. A federal order requiring milk silo testing then brought 45 states into surveillance . Authority plus a federally built system produced in months what persuasion had failed to produce in years.

We also know what does not work: coordination without authority.

Congress created the National Biosurveillance Integration Center at the Department of Homeland Security in 2007 to fuse human, animal, food and environmental data. By 2015, eight of 11 federal partners said its products helped them little or not at all, and only 5 of 19 shared data with it , citing legal restrictions. In 2023 it still lacked performance measures . The intelligence community’s biosecurity center was ordered terminated in December 2025.

NBIC’s mission was to integrate, and only to integrate. An integrator that cannot compel data, controls no budget, and commands no one writes reports.

Washington’s current answer is a slogan. In September 2025, the secretary of Health and Human Services wrote that CDC’s Biothreat Radar Detection System “ can spot pathogens like H5N1 or MERS early enough to prevent catastrophe. ” His department’s budget request called it “proposed.” Congress provided about $7 million of a roughly $100 million request . The 2027 request asks for funds again, while proposing to cut state and local preparedness grants from $735 million to $350 million; Health and Human Services has already terminated $11.4 billion in grants to the state and local departments that feed it.

The fix is structural, and the government already runs the model. The Joint Interagency Task Force South in Key West, which tracks drug trafficking across two oceans, is widely regarded as the gold standard for interagency operations: Five armed services, 13 law enforcement and intelligence agencies, and liaison officers from 20 nations work under one director who controls assets assigned to the mission while home agencies keep paying and promoting them.

Biosurveillance needs that — not another coordinating council.

Congress should charter a National Biosurveillance Task Force, housed at Health and Human Services and led by a civilian, with operational control of the people, systems and budgets that do federal biosurveillance today, matrixed from all the agencies named above, plus the Department of Veterans Affairs. It needs a single appropriation, so that the money follows the mission, and authority to set data standards enforced through the levers that already work, including Medicare conditions of participation, federal health IT certification, and Department of Agriculture orders.

States that want in can put their National Guard civil support teams, with mobile laboratories that identify biological agents , on the task force’s missions with federal funding, exactly as governors did for COVID testing in 2020 . The task force should build the system once, at federal expense, and give it to states, counties, tribes, hospitals, laboratories and companies for free with technical support, offering a simple bargain: contribute your data and get the integrated picture back within hours, plus preference in federal funding. Its charter should be de-identified data only. This is standards and reciprocity, not surveillance of citizens.

Start with food. Fifteen agencies administer at least 30 food safety laws ; the Government Accountability Office has called that “high risk” since 2007, and no national strategy exists. Foodborne outbreaks cross every agency line. Make them the proving ground.

A country that needed 2,900 cases and two deaths to register a disease it eliminated a generation ago is not prepared. Give the people who watch for it one picture, one budget and one commander to hold accountable.

Andrew G. Huff, Ph.D., is an epidemiologist, formerly of Michigan State University, and is affiliated with Risk Factor Research LLC. Previously he served as vice president at EcoHealth Alliance and as a senior member of the technical staff at Sandia National Laboratories. He is the author of “The Truth About Wuhan.”

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: The sprawling political transformation of Texas
articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon break down this week’s political news and answer questions from a live online audience.] Some 21 million people — more than two-thirds of all Texans — live in the triangle formed…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon break down this week’s political news and answer questions from a live online audience. ]

Some 21 million people — more than two-thirds of all Texans — live in the triangle formed by Houston, Dallas and San Antonio. It is a region the size of the state of New York with a population larger than 46 of the 50 states — and it’s still booming.

Demographers expect the Texas Triangle to continue to drive Lone Star State growth, with the region soon to have three quarters of the state population . It is a megalopolis that will one day surpass the Acela Corridor between Boston and Washington, D.C., as the Northeast withers and the Sun Belt blooms. In two or three decades, we may find that 20 percent of all Americans live in the triangle region.

If you followed those long, fat ribbons of concrete — I-35 from Dallas to San Antonio, I-10 from San Antonio to Houston and I-45 from Houston to Dallas — it would take you the better part of a day. Certainly, it will feel that way if you hit central Austin during rush hour traffic. But unlike the Northeast megalopolis, which is anchored by New York City, the Texas Triangle is all about the sprawl.

Places like little Waller County, northwest of Houston, keep recording shattering growth numbers, adding more than 13,000 residents in just the first five years of this decade . In 1990, Waller County was rural and agricultural with a population of about 23,000. Now it is almost entirely suburban with a population of more than 73,000. The three biggest cities in the triangle are stagnant or even — in the case of Dallas — shrinking, but the burbs keep booming.

Flat terrain, a year-round building season and typically permissive rules for zoning, etc. mean that while many places with growing economies chafe under housing shortages, the Texas Triangle offers 60,000 square miles of places to put shopping malls, subdivisions and schools.

There are serious political implications to all this upheaval. Texas was, as recently as 20 years ago, one of the least suburban large states in the country. Because of the nature of the dominant industries in the state — energy and agriculture — Texas was a state of small towns and big cities but much less of the in-between than places in California and the Northeast. But the 21st century boom has changed that. Texas will soon be a state that is 50 percent suburban, like those other places that boomed in the middle of the 20th century.

This is all happening at an inauspicious time for Texas Republicans. When former President George W. Bush made the leap from Texas governor to the presidency, he did so on the strength of Republicans in the suburbs — the so-called red wall that encircled America’s big, blue cities. If half of all voters lived in the burbs and the burbs were mostly Republican, you didn’t need to be Karl Rove to figure out where the action was.

But that changed in the Trump era, both because of what happened in the Republican Party but also what happened in the suburbs. It wasn’t just Texas that saw rapid growth in the suburbs in the first quarter of this century, which made those precincts younger and less white than they had traditionally been in the 1900s. Simultaneously, Republicans — first by accident and then very intentionally — shifted their pitch away from the core of their coalition back to the Eisenhower era in favor of working-class voters. Affluent, upwardly mobile, college-educated Americans — who had long leaned Republican and provided a base of high-propensity voters to weather midterm storms — were suddenly up for grabs.

After bleeding support in these places in 2016, 2018 and 2020, Republicans won them back narrowly in 2024. But as we stand on the precipice of the next midterm elections, it’s very obvious that the suburbanites have again flown the coop. What’s increasingly looking like a grim November for the GOP is going to mostly play out in the land of the strip malls and subdivisions.

The new Republican coalition would have been unbeatable in the old Texas but is increasingly vulnerable in the new Texas of megalopian sprawl. It’s a shift my colleague Sean Trende has been describing and documenting for years , and we may have finally arrived at the moment the state really starts to tip over.

None of this is to say that Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is sure to defeat Republican nominee Ken Paxton . When we look at the persistent, substantial gap between Paxton’s poor showing in the polls and that of other statewide Republican candidates — particularly Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — it’s obvious that we’re not at the demography-is-destiny phase of Democrats’ blue Texas ambitions. It still takes a candidate as bad as Paxton in a year for Democrats as good as this one to really put Texas in play.

But it is true that Talarico’s surprising durability in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988 wouldn’t be possible if it wasn’t for Texas’s astonishing demographic makeover. That itself should be a warning to the GOP about its future.

ON THE SIDE: PULLING STRINGS WITH YO-YO MA

Reporter Joshua Barone went on the road to see how the world’s most famous cellist, now 70, is strung for The New York Times : “It isn’t easy to interview Yo-Yo Ma . Not because he is one of the most famous musicians alive, a cellist who has been playing for world leaders since he was 7. Nor because he tends to answer questions with long stories rather than sound bites. … He is a sincerely committed humanist in a time that more readily rewards cynicism. … When he speaks about immigration or education, he avoids the brash, polarizing rhetoric that reigns today, subtly treating these topics as matters of ethics rather than politics. ‘There’s nobody that’s not interesting,’ he said by way of explanation during a recent interview at his hotel while performing in Denver … I quickly learned what former President Barack Obama meant when he once said of Ma, ‘For every question you ask him, he asks you two in return.’”

PRIME CUTS: SENATE AD WARS AND A BALKY BALLOT BLOCKADE

Pro-Collins super PAC pushes transgender sports to the fore: Axios : “A super PAC working to reelect Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) is plowing $1.1 million into an ad campaign attacking Democrat Troy Jackson for supporting state legislation that allows transgender women to be housed in women’s prisons. The ad is the latest example of Republicans using visceral attacks on transgender policies to draw sharp contrasts with Democrats on a hot-button cultural issue. But for the first time this cycle, Republicans are taking the transgender issue into a blue-state Senate race. The strategy behind the two-week blitz from Pine Tree Results is clear: drive Jackson’s negatives higher. ‘As Senate president, Jackson signed the bill requiring state prisons to house biological men if they identify as female with women prisoners,’ the narrator says.”

80-year-old progressive Ed Markey wins Massachusetts Senate primary: The Hill : “ Seth Moulton , a 47-year-old who’s served in the House for six terms, had lodged a generational change campaign against Ed Markey , an 80-year-old who served 20 terms in the House and is seeking a third term in the Senate. But Markey emerged victorious in Tuesday’s primary, teeing him up for another six years representing the solidly blue state in the upper chamber alongside fellow Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.). He will face off against Republican John Deaton , who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, in November. … Former President Biden ’s exit from the 2024 race amid health concerns and the recent passing of multiple congressional Democrats in office have invigorated younger candidates who argue that older lawmakers are out-of-touch with the party. But unlike some high-profile contests that saw the younger challengers running to the left of the incumbents, Markey was seen by many as the more progressive in the race.”

Ponzi scheme scandal further dims Georgia GOP’s hopes: The Wall Street Journal : “ James McMaster , 94 years old, lost about $1.3 million in the collapse of First Liberty Building & Loan, the Georgia investment firm built by a family of Republican power brokers. He recently got a call to contribute to a GOP campaign. ‘I said, “OK, let me tell you. Here’s where I’m at,”‘ McMaster said. ‘When you get all the politicians that have received funds from them and get them to return them, then maybe we can talk.’ Nationally, Republicans face familiar midterm headwinds, from inflation to the war with Iran. Georgia’s GOP is contending with a problem notable to the Peach State: a $140-million Ponzi-scheme scandal that has ruptured the party’s ultraconservative wing. … Some Republicans worry the controversy will cloud voters’ view of a state GOP that has been troubled by infighting and turmoil since 2020. Rusty Paul , a former state GOP chair, said the Frosts’ abrupt exit from state Republican politics could be healthy for the party in the long run. ‘It removes a thorn from the body Republican,’ he said.”

El-Sayed tries ‘Love Island’ pitch to Michiganders: Yahoo News : “ Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed turned his campaign into a reality TV audition Tuesday, releasing a Love Island -inspired TikTok that promoted his progressive platform while poking fun at Republican attacks on his name and his supposed disdain for football. The slick video casts the 41-year-old as the latest cast member desperate for a turn on ‘Senate Island,’ borrowing the high-energy sun-soaked format of the hit dating show’s contestant introductions to make his pitch to Michigan voters. … With pop singer Raye’s hit ‘Where the Hell is My Husband!’ playing in the background, El-Sayed appears against flashing pink and yellow backdrops surrounded by beach balls and inflatables. ‘I’m Abdul El-Sayed. I’m 41 years old, and I’m from Ann Arbor, Michigan,’ he begins, before addressing a line of attack Republicans have increasingly aimed at him. ‘Oh, my name. Yeah, I love my name,’ El-Sayed says. ‘My people don’t know this. It means ‘servant leader.’ Right here on my bracelet.’”

New TV ads from Paxton make Talarico out to be a Chinese sympathizer: Politico : “Allies of Texas GOP Senate hopeful Ken Paxton are planning a $15 million ad campaign starting Tuesday, the first major ad buy on behalf of Paxton in his battleground matchup with Democrat James Talarico . Two new ads from Lone Star Liberty PAC, the pro-Paxton super PAC, will air across 18 markets across Texas over the ensuing two weeks. They mark Paxton’s first significant foray on to the airwaves, jolting a campaign that has been clouded by concerns over Talarico’s massive cash advantage and Paxton’s electability. … The other new advertisement accuses Talarico of aiding China’s growth at the expense of Texas residents, pointing to the Democrat’s vote against restrictions on Chinese investments, and argues that a Chinese billionaire’s ownership of land near Laughlin Air Force Base presents national security concerns. ‘China’s got Talarico. Texas needs Ken Paxton,’ the ad says.”

Talarico cries foul over closure of polling locations: The Associated Press : “A plan in one of Texas’ largest counties to use dozens fewer polling locations than in previous years is drawing protests from Democrats who say the reductions could create confusion in the November midterm elections. The proposal, set for a vote Tuesday, would reduce the number of polling locations across booming Tarrant County, which borders Dallas and includes Fort Worth. County officials say the plan would save resources by eliminating low-turnout sites, noting voters would still have more than 200 locations where they could cast ballots. Texas’ third-largest county is home to more than 2 million people and a key battleground in the U.S. Senate race between Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton . On Sunday, Talarico urged the county to reject the proposal. ‘The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able vote easily,’ Talarico said at a news conference.”

USPS quickly rolls out ballot crackdown plan: The New York Times : “The U.S. Postal Service has been swiftly developing a complex screening system for mail-in ballots ahead of this year’s midterm elections, despite ongoing legal wranglings over President Trump ’s executive order to restrict voting by mail. The new system, which requires states to tell the Postal Service which voters will be sent ballots so they can be verified before delivery, shows how aggressively the Postal Service is moving to deliver on the president’s directive ahead of the upcoming elections, which could tip the scales of power in Congress. The agency’s efforts to set up a way to restrict who gets mail ballots, even as the matter is being fought over in the courts, could cause confusion among voters and undermine confidence in the Postal Service as states are close to getting ballots out the door, current and former state officials said. If the new screening system is ultimately put in place, it could jeopardize the ability of people to receive and cast their ballots, they said.”

Whistleblower says Trump ballot blockade may crash system : The Hill: “A whistleblower on Monday warned that the U.S. Postal Service’s computer system is riddled with errors and could jeopardize mail-in voting in the November midterm elections, according to a statement from Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). The individual said the Postal Service has attempted to build a complex system over a three-month time frame, beginning on or around June 15, to be used for the midterms, a process that typically takes a year or longer. The work was expected to stop amid a federal judge’s ruling that temporarily halted President Trump ’s executive order to limit voting by mail, a ruling that the Trump administration has appealed. … The order introduces a portal for the Postal Service to screen ballots submitted by state election officials. The whistleblower said standard and needed testing had been eliminated and that it created ‘the substantial risk of a ‘catastrophic failure’ of the system that could ‘derail the midterm elections,’ Blumenthal said, quoting the whistleblower.”

articles.title: Top DHS lawyer turns tables on 128 ex-judges after Bar declines ‘Worst of the Worst’ complaint
articles.summary: James Percival compared the 128 former judges' Florida Bar complaint to the Hunter Biden laptop controversy, calling the filing frivolous "Bar-fare."
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: DHS General Counsel James Percival is turning a complaint from 128 former judges back on its signers, calling on the Florida Bar to scrutinize those among them who are Bar members after it declined to investigate him. The Bar said it does not investigate or prosecute sitting officers appointed under the U.S. Constitution while they are in office, a position Percival argued the complainants should have known before challenging his "Worst of the Worst Judges" series. Percival accused the Florida Bar members who joined the complaint of potentially abusing the disciplinary process for political purposes, arguing their filing was frivolous and dubbing the tactic "Bar-fare." "The 128 former judges are sort of an example of a tactic the left has used for a long time," Percival told Fox News Digital, comparing their appeal to professional authority to the 2020 controversy involving 51 former intelligence officials and Hunter Biden’s laptop. DHS EVISCERATES MEDIA FOR ‘ABSOLUTE ABSURDITY’ OVER CONCERN ABOUT ‘WORST OF THE WORST’ ACTIVIST JUDGES LIST Percival pointed to the Florida Bar's previous handling of a complaint involving former Attorney General Pam Bondi, arguing that they already signaled refusal to probe sitting presidential appointees. "[W]hat these 128 former judges did was frivolous, and they were on notice that it was frivolous because the Florida Bar is very clear about this. So, it's ‘Bar-fare’," he said, playing on the term "lawfare." LIBERAL LAW PROFESSOR BREAKS WITH OBAMA JUDGE OVER TRUMP LAWYER CRACKDOWN: ‘I REFUSE TO TEACH’ IT Percival said the same tactic has been used elsewhere, including the Hunter Biden laptop controversy and the way dissent over COVID-era restrictions was met with echoes of "trust the experts." "The left has just like often hid behind this veneer, this prestige [of expertise] and they've gotten people who carry weight to carry their water for them. And I really think the emperor has no clothes on this, but we have to call it out and expose it." When the political left does not want to publicly debate the merits of their assertion, they get figures who appear authoritative to shut down dissent, he said. The comments came after rule-of-law groups Democracy Defenders Fund, Lawyers Defending American Democracy and 128 former federal and state judges filed a 24-page complaint accusing Percival of violating Florida's rules governing statements about judges. The complaint alleged that Percival, a licensed Florida attorney, violated ethics rules through "public attacks on sitting judges." "His statements mischaracterized the judges’ rulings and assailed their character and integrity. The ethics rules exist for a reason: Baseless attacks on judges by lawyers and public officials can undermine confidence in the courts and heighten the risk of physical threats against judges," Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement after the Bar declined to investigate the complaint. Former Florida Supreme Court Chief Justice Peggy Quince, an appointee of Democratic ex-Gov. Lawton Chiles, led the judges’ consortium. The complaint focuses on four judges featured in Percival's "Worst of the Worst" posts, whom he accused of actions including "open defiance of the Supreme Court," "judicial sabotage" and "judicial micromanagement." SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS The cases involved disputes over Temporary Protected Status, the government's handling of Kilmar Ábrego García and DHS use-of-force policies. The complaint also referenced an article written by Percival condemning former President Joe Biden and a Rhode Island judge he appointed after an illegal immigrant whom DHS said had an international warrant for homicide was ordered released. Percival said the activist judges themselves are the ones who are being a "disservice to the judiciary." He argued that judges know their district court rulings can delay executive action when they cannot be immediately appealed. As for the complainants, Percival said those who are themselves members of the Florida Bar should face scrutiny over whether they abused the complaint process for political purposes. The Bar provided Fox News Digital a copy of its response sent to the Framingham, Massachusetts, address listed for the collective complainants. Bar Counsel Christopher Wackes wrote his group does not investigate or prosecute "sitting officers appointed under the U.S. Constitution while they are in office." Wackes said any action could "encroach on the authority of the federal government." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He quipped situations like the bar complaint show he is over the proverbial target: "[I]f people are this upset about what I'm doing, it must be having an effect that they don't like, which really just encourages me to keep going," he said, pressing conservatives to fight for their causes despite the knowledge the left will "try to ruin your life." Fox News Digital's Kiera McDonald contributed to this report.

articles.title: White House puts Trump-style classic video games on website ahead of midterms

Deport. Fill a Trump Account,” the White House said on social media about the games’ launch. Two games focus on the Trump administration’s…
articles.body:
The White House late Thursday unveiled a new online arcade on its website featuring five games that focus on different Trump administration policies ahead of the 2026 midterm election.

“Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account,” the White House said on social media about the games’ launch.

Two games focus on the Trump administration’s immigration policy, with Rio Run depicting President Trump on a “border patrol along the Rio Grande” and Build the Wall instructing users to “protect the border from the coming horde.” Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained almost 50,000 people in July, the highest the figure had been since Trump took office.

ICE and Customs and Border Protection have been able to expand their enforcement across the country during Trump’s second term with operations such as February’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota, called Operation Metro Surge. The agencies have also invested heavily in their officers as Trump rolls back deportation protections for several migrant groups.

Another game, Trump Savings Tycoon, gives players a net with which to grab money and “fill your kids'” Trump savings accounts — a newborn investment plan that offers $1,000 to every child enrolled in the program from the federal government.

More than 6 million children have been signed up for Trump accounts since the program launched, according to the Treasury Department .

The game notably shows monuments on the National Mall, where Trump has sought to undergo renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Flappy Bill also features the National Mall , with a bald eagle carrying legislation attempting to avoid obstacles. In Supply Line, players sort food on an assembly line and are instructed to reject items that do not match “Make America Healthy Again” standards.

The White House teased that there could be more games to come.

articles.title: Supreme Court hands Trump another win — a monkey wrench into voting by mail
articles.summary: The court has put additional Trump wins on the scoreboard, leaving the public with little confidence that it is anything other than partisan.
articles.body:
Justice Elena Kagan, an avowed institutionalist, has said it is a “bad rap” that the Supreme Court is in the tank for President Trump. She may have been thinking of the tariff and birthright citizenship cases, in which majorities ruled against his policy initiatives.

But in recent weeks, in the White House ballroom and vote-by-mail cases, the court has put additional Trump wins on the scoreboard, leaving the public with little confidence that it is anything other than partisan.

In the latest development, the court paved the way for Trump to proceed with an executive order that directs the states and the Department of Homeland Security to create “state citizenship lists” to eliminate noncitizens from voter rolls. The U.S. Postal Service will decide who gets a mail-in ballot. The problem is that under the Constitution, it is states that are supposed to decide, not the federal government.

Studies show that nearly one in three Americans voted by mail in the 2024 general election, about one in four registered Democrats and one in five registered Republicans. Trump has voted by mail on numerous occasions.

But more recently, voting by mail has become a Trump piñata.

The court’s majority held Trump was likely to “suffer irreparable harm” unless it lifted a temporary freeze imposed by lower courts. Accordingly, in a case brought by 23 blue states against Trump, it paused an injunction entered by Obama-appointed Boston Federal Judge Indira Talwani barring the federal government from applying provisions of the executive order in the November midterm elections.

A separate ruling by the same judge, in another case filed by the League of Women Voters, temporarily restrains the postal service from implementing the executive order. Whether that ruling will withstand Supreme Court scrutiny remains to be seen.

The majority opinion said it was too soon for courts to consider the states’ challenge because the Postal Service order has not yet been finalized — a legal doctrine known as “ripeness.” But a whistleblower later alleged the agency is moving forward with a “secretive, rushed” effort to carry out Trump’s order, which could lead to a “catastrophic failure” in the mail ballot system ahead of the midterms. This means that millions of voters might be unable to receive their ballots in a timely manner, or at all.

The justices stressed that the preliminary order was not a final decision about whether the administration’s order is legal if and when the plans are complete.

The court’s three Democratic appointees dissented. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson accused the majority of “taking its eye off the ball.” The result, she said , is a “Kafkaesque nightmare.” Although the court has made clear that “even valid election-related legal claims can come too late,” she argued, the majority now indicates “that such claims can also come too early.”

Section one of Trump’s executive order instructs Homeland Security to create lists of adult U.S. citizens in each state and to send those lists to states at least 60 days before an election.

Section three requires states to give the U.S. Postal Service a curated list of voters to whom the states intend to send mail ballots (presupposing that the states will agree to furnish such lists and that the lists are complete). The Trump order directs the postal service to refuse to deliver mail-in ballots to individuals who don’t appear on the lists.

A Court of Appeals declined to pause Talwani’s order while the litigation continued. It stressed that neither the federal government nor 12 red states joining the case on Trump’s side had argued that the executive order was legal.

The majority also found that the government would suffer irreparable harm if Talwani’s order is not paused now. Even if its ruling is eventually reversed, the majority emphasized , it “would come too late for the 2026 midterms.” In contrast, the majority said, the states would not be harmed from putting Talwani’s order on hold, because the executive order doesn’t require them to do anything.

But what about the requirement to produce the lists?

In a dissenting opinion joined by Kagan, Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote that the government was trying to “have it both ways.” On one hand, she observed, the majority “says it was speculative to think there would be a final rule at all when this suit was filed, seemingly accepting the government’s representation that it may not actually implement the Executive Order.” But the government “insists that it seeks to implement the Executive Order immediately for purposes of establishing irreparable harm.”

Jackson’s dissent brings to mind the “ Purcell principle ” — the notion that, close to election day, federal courts should do nothing rather than issue coercive orders changing the rules for who can vote.

If the court uses Purcell to allow the illegal executive order to survive, the decision, says legal scholar Stephen Vladeck , “would be as indefensible and anti-democratic a ruling as the court has handed down in a very long time.”

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

North Carolina is set to begin mailing general election absentee ballots on Friday, even as the Trump administration has moved to restrict voting by mail.

The administration is appealing a federal judge’s ruling that stops it from moving forward with voting restrictions established by executive order for at least for one more week. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to lift the block.

And North Carolina’s State Board of Elections will meet at 9 a.m. EDT to offer guidance on mailing ballots.

The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs last month, a stronger-than-expected showing.

Stars and Stripes staffers whom the Pentagon wants to fire will be in a Washington court on Friday morning to fight the termination notices.

President Trump has a policy meeting and will sign an executive order on Friday before heading to New Jersey for the holiday weekend.

articles.title: Trump’s war on free speech doesn’t just affect Democrats
articles.summary: So if we can punish Kristen Welker, it will soon be open season on “unfairness” in the media and on “fake news.” And that goes for both sides of the political spectrum.
articles.body:
Normally, I’m a big critic of President Trump’s, but you’ve got to give him credit for taking a robust stand for media accuracy, demanding that Kristen Welker be punished by the Federal Communications Commission for saying that Trump’s primary endorsements had yielded “some mixed results.”

The president didn’t pull any punches . “How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? … Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment. … The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously.”

Carr can do it, too. There is an FCC policy that prohibits “news distortion” in over-the-air broadcasts. That policy has been around for more than 50 years, but was seldom invoked until Trump and Carr decided to revive and strengthen it.

There is almost no case law on this policy. And even in its original form, it is fairly dubious, First Amendment-wise. So it is important that Trump and Carr do whatever they can to get this policy well-established while they have the chance.

That’s all the more true since, in the past, this rule has been narrowly construed . Since the Reagan administration, the FCC invoked it just one time, when NBC rigged some gas tanks to explode so they’d get better footage for an investigative news segment.

Trump’s new “unfairness doctrine” goes well beyond that, seeking to sanction broadcasters who present “fake news” that’s unfairly critical of either him or the government. Carr’s first serious effort to implement this expanded “distortion” doctrine was an attempt to punish late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, for what Carr said appeared to be an intentional effort to mislead the public about the political leanings of Charlie Kirk’s assassin.

Welker’s alleged misstatement — I say “alleged” because she was arguably correct — was far more anodyne than that. She merely observed that Trump’s primary endorsements didn’t invariably win their primaries. Even if it was wrong, this hardly classifies as a “threat to our country,” regardless of what the president might say.

So if we can punish Kristen Welker, it will soon be open season on “unfairness” in the media and on “fake news.” This is going to be a huge help to any future Democratic president — perhaps Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ? — who wants to go after the conspiracy theories and “purposeful inaccuracies” in right-wing media.

AM talk radio is the cornerstone of conservative media. And it’s on the public airways — and subject to the same FCC rules — just like NBC is. Radio shows like the now-defunct Infowars would be banned under the new doctrine. Heck, if the FCC had been serious about enforcement, it would have been banned under the old doctrine. Infowars was infamous for pushing dangerous and obviously bonkers conspiracy theories.

But Infowars would just be the tip of the iceberg. Listen to conservative stalwarts like Sean Hannity or Mark Levin and you’ll probably hear them giving air time to claims far more dubious than Welker’s on an hourly basis. Hannity promoted Trump’s claims that the election was stolen even though he knew they were lies. Levin — and lots of other broadcasters — went on at length about the “Biden crime family.”

None of this would be allowed under the new “unfairness doctrine.” All these shows would be forced off the air. Sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander so, of course, Republicans would have no objections to any future Democratic president’s efforts to clean up the media, just as they are refusing to defend Welker now.

Is that what you want, Republicans? Because that is what you are going to get. Donald Trump doesn’t care about you or the future of the GOP. He is a political solipsist and, as far as he is concerned, the world ends when he leaves office. That’s why he is constantly demanding Republicans eliminate the filibuster and undermining America’s faith in elections . When he is no longer president, none of the resulting carnage will affect him. Once conservative media is no longer useful to him — and no longer devoted to singing his praises — Trump could not care less.

MAGA Republicans enjoy “ liberal tears ” but it’s not just liberals who are suffering. The blowback from Trump’s buffoonery is affecting everyone from union workers in Manhattan to farmers in Kansas. We’re all paying higher food and gas prices, and we’re spending tens of billions on a new unplanned and unwinnable forever war. Now Trump wants to add the First Amendment to the wreckage.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney who served as Southern California chair for John McCain’s primary campaign in 2008.

articles.title: FCC asks court to reject Disney lawsuit over ABC stations’ licenses
articles.summary: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is asking a federal judge to toss a lawsuit brought by Disney and ABC over the agency’s move to call several of the network’s local stations for early license renewal. In a filing with the court made public Thursday, lawyers for the FCC argued the Disney suit is premature and…
articles.body:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is asking a federal judge to toss a lawsuit brought by Disney and ABC over the agency’s move to call several of the network’s local stations for early license renewal.

In a filing with the court made public Thursday, lawyers for the FCC argued the Disney suit is premature and obstructs what it characterized as a necessary part of its investigation into the company’s diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) hiring policies.

Disney contends the commission is attempting to stifle its First Amendment rights on the basis of the content broadcast on ABC.

“This would only hobble the Commission’s efforts to investigate and resolve serious allegations that Disney has engaged in unlawful discrimination, and from otherwise ensuring that Disney’s stations are serving the public interest,” the agency wrote in its filing. “Plaintiffs, in return, would only free themselves from the burdens of proving their case in administrative proceedings.”

Disney sued the FCC last month after the commission called the licenses of several local stations in major markets across the country up for renewal, an unusual move that unsettled press freedom activists and some elected Democrats.

It followed months of tension between the Trump administration and one of the country’s largest broadcasters, which wrote in its complaint that the FCC under President Trump has sent a “message to every media company in the country” — that they should “tell only the stories the Administration deems favorable, or face the coercive machinery of the federal government.”

“In such a world, the press could in no way be described as free,” the company wrote. “The FCC Chairman has left little doubt that this is his goal.”

In a statement to The Hill, an FCC spokesperson said, “Disney filed a meritless lawsuit in an effort to stop the FCC’s ongoing investigation into allegations that Disney violated the law.”

“The FCC has developed a voluminous record, and it will continue to follow the facts and the law wherever they lead,” the spokesperson continued Friday. “As the FCC’s motion to dismiss shows, Disney filed its meritless case in the wrong court at the wrong time based on erroneous legal and factual assertions.”

FCC Chair Brendan Carr, a frequent critic of mainstream media outlets, has questioned whether ABC is using airwaves regulated by the agency in the “public interest” and called for the firing of the network’s late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over jokes he made about the president and the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

He has separately vowed to investigate major media companies over their DEI initiatives, defending his department’s investigation of those practices.

“The balance of equities and the public interest just as clearly weigh against enjoining the Commission’s investigation. Broadcasters are highly regulated parties subject to the Commission’s comprehensive oversight,” the FCC wrote as part of its filing this week.

“Licenses grant them exclusive access — awarded for free — to highly valuable portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, an important and finite public resource,” it added.

articles.body:
President Trump said late Thursday that Maria Bartiromo’s fans will not be happy that the host is out at Fox News.

“I can’t believe Maria Bartiromo is no longer going to have her great show(s) on FoxNews/Business,” the president wrote on Truth Social . “Three different shows, always number one. Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior.”

“Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria,” he added.

Bartiromo worked at Fox Business for just more than 12 years and grew to be one of Trump’s most vocal supporters on the network. Before that, she worked as a financial journalist for 20 years at CNBC, where she won an Emmy Award for a documentary about Google.

Fox abruptly announced that the final episode of “Mornings with Maria” aired Thursday morning and that the show would be called “Mornings with Fox Business” beginning Friday and feature rotating hosts.

The network will also rename “Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street” to “FBN’s Wall Street,” with a new host.

Fox News gave few details on what led to Bartiromo’s departure.

“We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 1/2 years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” it said in a short statement .

While at Fox News, Bartiromo was sued by voting machine company Smartmatic in 2021, alongside former host Jeanine Pirro, who is now U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia.

Smartmatic argued that Fox and its hosts caused financial harm to the company by promoting election fraud claims during the 2020 election — though Bartiromo vehemently denied the allegation.

Bartiromo and Fox News tried to dismiss the lawsuit, saying the “headline-seeking, multi-billion-dollar lawsuit thus should be seen—and rejected—for what it is: an unconstitutional attempt by a money-losing company … to try to refill its coffers at the expense of our constitutional traditions.”

She was also deposed in another case against Fox involving Dominion Voting Systems — another election voting machine company — after hosting guests who argued similar election fraud claims.

Bartiromo notably booked Trump and his allies at the time on her “Sunday Morning Futures” show on several occasions after the 2020 election while they contested former President Biden’s win in court and in the media.

articles.title: ICE officer charged with lying about shooting turns himself in: Reports
articles.summary: An immigration officer is facing federal charges for making false statements about the shooting of a Venezuelan migrant during the Trump administration’s deportation crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, several outlets reported. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Christian Castro was in custody in Texas on Thursday evening after a federal grand jury indicted Castro…
articles.body:
An immigration officer is facing federal charges for making false statements about the shooting of a Venezuelan migrant during the Trump administration’s deportation crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, several outlets reported.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Christian Castro was in custody in Texas on Thursday evening after a federal grand jury indicted Castro on six counts making materially false statements to investigators.

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and ICE for comment.

Castro also faces state assault charges in Minnesota for shooting and wounding Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The state charges also include falsely reporting a crime after Castro allegedly told his superiors at DHS that Sosa-Celis and other people attacked him with a snow shovel and a broom — claims disproven by video evidence.

The federal charges follow the officer’s release last week after spending 90 days in a Texas county jail. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) refused to sign extradition papers requested by Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) so he could face charges there.

Mary Moriarty, county attorney for Minnesota’s Hennepin County, said in a statement shared with The Hill that Castro had been arrested again in Texas and said she expected the officer would “appear in federal court” there and eventually in Minnesota.

“Despite Gov. Abbott’s best efforts to shield Mr. Castro, we will see him soon,” she added.

Castro is the first federal immigration officer to be prosecuted by the Justice Department for actions related to the Trump administration’s Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota earlier this year.

The massive immigration crackdown effort, in which thousands of federal troops were deployed to the Twin Cities, sparked controversy after immigration officers shot and killed two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Robin Wolpert, an attorney for Sosa-Celis, told The Associated Press in a statement that the Justice Department “grossly undercharged this case,” following ProPublica’s reporting earlier this week that found department officials reportedly blocked a prosecutor’s push to bring more serious charges against Castro.

“Mr. Sosa Celis wants Mr. Castro to be held fully accountable for his crimes,” Wolpert said, according to the AP.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Minnesota said in a statement Thursday that it will represent Sosa-Celis in his lawsuit against the Trump administration, in which he will seek damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act.

“Today’s indictment is not enough,” the group’s deputy legal director, Catherine Ahlin-Halverson, said in a statement. “Julio was shot by Christian Castro, arrested, and falsely prosecuted.”

“The enormity of what happened to him is so great, and such an egregious violation of his fundamental rights, that he can never be made whole,” she continued. “We must demand that our system do better to hold these federal agents accountable to him, and to all of us, and that is why we are bringing this administrative claim on his behalf.”

articles.title: Former Trump Cabinet official had 'inappropriately close' relationship with bodyguard, IG finds
articles.summary: Lori Chavez-DeRemer allegedly ordered a security agent to throw cash at a stripper during an Oregon trip, a Department of Labor OIG report says.
articles.body: Former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer allegedly had an inappropriate relationship with her bodyguard and created a hostile work environment for her subordinates, according to a Thursday report from the Department of Labor's (DOL's) Office of the Inspector General (OIG). The report cites one incident in which Chavez-DeRemer allegedly ordered a member of her security detail to throw cash at a stripper. Chavez-DeRemer, who resigned her position in April, had been under investigation after the OIG received an anonymous complaint in January. That complaint alleged Chavez-DeRemer's inappropriate relationship with the assistant special agent-in-charge (ASAIC) of her department's Division of Protective Operations (DPO), who the report did not name. TRUMP TAPS ACTING LABOR SECRETARY KEITH SONDERLING FOR PERMANENT ROLE PENDING SENATE CONFIRMATION The complaint also alleged that Chavez-DeRemer, her chief of staff, Jihun Han, and deputy chief of staff, Rebecca Wright, created a hostile work environment and regularly drank alcohol on DOL property and during work hours. The OIG interviewed 38 witnesses who described the DOL work environment as "toxic, intimidating and humiliating." The witnesses reported that Chavez-DeRemer, Han and Wright "openly discussed employee performance matters in the presence of other staff, including details of performance-related meetings and whether those employees had cried during the meetings." HIGH-RANKING DHS OFFICIAL SIDELINED OVER ALLEGATIONS OF 'SUGAR DADDY' RELATIONSHIP, LUXE GIFTS AND DRUG USE Witnesses also told the OIG that Chavez-DeRemer's alleged relationship with the ASAIC also contributed to the hostile work environment. During an April trip to Oregon, the ASAIC complied with Chavez-DeRemer's request to make an unplanned, off-the-record stop at "an establishment that was determined upon entry to feature partially nude dancers," according to the report. The ASAIC assigned Chavez-DeRemer's driver to enter the establishment with her, and, according to the report, she handed the driver a stack of cash and instructed him to give it to one of the dancers. When the driver refused, the ASAIC instructed him to comply. "Chavez-DeRemer then took additional money from her purse and asked the agent to drop the bills one by one onto the partially nude woman. The agent again hesitated and sought intervention from ASAIC 1, who told him to follow Chavez-DeRemer's instructions," according to the report. The complaint and subsequent investigation also determined that the ASAIC's alleged inappropriate relationship with the former labor secretary, who is married, affected his job performance. "ASAIC 1 allegedly focused on his interactions with Chavez-DeRemer, monitored her interactions with other agents, and reduced the presence of other DPO personnel to create opportunities to be alone with her, resulting in reduced protective coverage for the Secretary," the report read. COURT FILINGS REVEAL KYRSTEN SINEMA HAD SEX MULTIPLE TIMES WITH MARRIED BODYGUARD WHILE SERVING AS SENATOR The pair reportedly grew immediately close upon Chavez-DeRemer's arrival at the department in March 2025, communicating often through the encrypted messaging app Signal in off-duty hours and about non-operational subjects. Another witness described observing Chavez-DeRemer massaging the ASAIC's shoulders in a car after he had finished a driving shift. When she asked if he was tired, he allegedly responded that he was "solid as a rock," and the pair both laughed. "The witness interpreted the comment as sexual innuendo," the report read. MARRIED FEDERAL JUDGE REPEATEDLY HAD COURTHOUSE SEX WITH LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICER, COMPLAINT ALLEGES Other witnesses described the pair walking arm in arm after leaving an event at Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins' home. After opening the investigation, the OIG surveilled Chavez-Deremer's Washington, D.C., home and found the ASAIC entering her residence through a back door on repeated occasions. FEDERAL JUDGE WHO HAD SEX IN CHAMBERS APOLOGIZES TO FORMER CLERK AS IMPEACHMENT PUSH RAMPS UP After reports that the ASAIC was breaking chain-of-command protocol by attending meetings with Chavez-DeRemer's chief of staff and deputy chief of staff without his Special Agent in Charge's (SAIC) knowledge, the SAIC recommended he take a leave of absence. However, the SAIC did not escalate beyond this recommendation for fear she herself would be terminated. "ASAIC 1 declined the suggestion to take leave and agreed that the SAIC taking action to limit his travel with Chavez-DeRemer could result in the SAIC’s removal," the report read.
